problems.stem: A candidate uploads a polished lesson plan to the portfolio and labels it "evidence of differentiation." What turns that artifact into actual evidence?
options: Making the plan look more professional.
Pairing it with the claim it supports, the part of the plan that shows differentiation, and the outcome it produced.
Uploading it in a higher-resolution format.
Adding more lessons to the folder.
problems.explanation: An artifact is not self-evident. It becomes portfolio evidence only when paired with the claim, the warranting detail, and the result.

problems.stem: A reflection states "This entry demonstrates that I use assessment data to drive instruction." Which addition gives the claim a warrant?
options: Repeating the claim in stronger words.
Pointing to the exit-ticket data and the next-day revision the data produced, both visible in the attached artifact.
Saying the candidate strongly believes in data.
Adding more standards to the same claim.
problems.explanation: A claim needs a warrant: the specific moment in the evidence that shows it. Without that location, the claim is an assertion.

problems.stem: A candidate tags a single TeachGen@i-assisted lesson plan to five competencies: planning, differentiation, assessment, technology integration, and family communication. Why is a reviewer right to be skeptical?
options: AI-assisted plans can never be portfolio evidence.
One artifact rarely genuinely demonstrates five unrelated competencies; overclaiming weakens the entries that are real.
Five is too few competencies for one plan.
Technology integration cannot appear in a lesson plan.
problems.explanation: Each claim should match the artifact that truly shows it. Stretching one plan across many standards dilutes credibility.

problems.stem: Which portfolio entry, mapped on the Design Tension Studio map, is strongest for an external reviewer to audit?
options: A clean lesson plan with the label "good teaching."

A claim (uses formative data to revise), the warrant (annotated exit tickets plus the revised next-day opener), the outcome (area-perimeter errors dropped from six to one the following day), and a note that a second standard was deliberately not claimed because this artifact does not show it.
Five competencies tagged to one screenshot.
A reflection that says the lesson went well.
problems.explanation: The strongest entry pairs one claim with a located warrant and an outcome, and resists overclaiming, which is exactly what a reviewer can verify.

problems.stem: Provide a concise response that demonstrates this learning objective: Document a bounded AI/software support move with accepted and rejected suggestions.
problems.expected_answer: The response accurately demonstrates the section objective: Document a bounded AI/software support move with accepted and rejected suggestions, using relevant section concepts, evidence, or calculations.
problems.explanation: This direct-evidence item is used when no closed-response item adequately samples the objective. Score it with the section concepts and worked examples as the rubric.
